meta.titre: Amines and Amides: preparation, basicity and the Hofmann degradation

sections.contenu_markdown: The sharp smell of fish left too long in the sun at a Douala market comes from amines such as trimethylamine, small basic molecules that evaporate easily. A squeeze of lemon on the fish reduces the smell because the acid turns the volatile amine into an odourless salt. The same nitrogen chemistry gives amides: the fishing nets sold on the same stalls are made of nylon, a polyamide, and the peptide links in the proteins of the fish itself are amide links. At GCE Advanced Level you must know how amines and amides are made, why amines are bases and amides are not, and how the Hofmann degradation shortens a carbon chain by one carbon.

items: Ammonia, NH3, has a lone pair on the nitrogen atom and acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base by accepting a proton.
A nucleophile donates a lone pair of electrons to an electron-deficient carbon atom, as in the substitution of a halogenoalkane.
Acyl chlorides are very reactive carboxylic acid derivatives made from carboxylic acids.
A lone pair that is delocalised into a pi system or onto a C=O group is less available to bond to a proton.

sections.titre: Classification, preparation, basicity and reactions of amines and amides
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Structure.** Amines are derived from ammonia by replacing hydrogen atoms with alkyl or aryl groups: primary $\mathrm{RNH_2}$, secondary $\mathrm{R_2NH}$, tertiary $\mathrm{R_3N}$ (the class is the number of carbon groups attached to nitrogen). A primary amide contains $\mathrm{-CONH_2}$, for example ethanamide $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}$.

**Making amines.**

- A halogenoalkane is heated with a large excess of ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br + 2NH_3 \to CH_3CH_2NH_2 + NH_4Br}$. The excess of ammonia is essential: the amine formed is also a nucleophile and would attack more halogenoalkane, giving secondary and tertiary amines and finally a quaternary ammonium salt.
- A nitrile is reduced with $\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ in dry ether, or with $\mathrm{H_2}$ and a nickel catalyst: $\mathrm{RC{\equiv}N \to RCH_2NH_2}$. The chain gains one carbon atom.
- Nitrobenzene is reduced by heating with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid; aqueous sodium hydroxide is then added to release phenylamine from its salt.
- An amide is converted to an amine with one carbon less by the Hofmann degradation (see the variants).

**Making amides.** An acyl chloride reacts with concentrated ammonia, or with a primary amine, at room temperature: $\mathrm{CH_3COCl + 2NH_3 \to CH_3CONH_2 + NH_4Cl}$.

**Basicity.** An amine is a weak base because the lone pair on nitrogen accepts a proton: $\mathrm{RNH_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons RNH_3^+ + OH^-}$. The order of base strength is

$$\text{ethylamine} > \text{ammonia} > \text{phenylamine} > \text{ethanamide (neutral)}$$

- In ethylamine the alkyl group pushes electron density towards nitrogen, so the lone pair is more available than in ammonia.
- In phenylamine the lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available.
- In an amide the lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl group, so amides do not accept protons appreciably and are neutral to litmus.

Amines are soluble in water when small because they form hydrogen bonds, and they react with acids to form soluble ionic salts, for example $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2 + HCl \to CH_3CH_2NH_3^+Cl^-}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: To convert an amide into a primary amine that has one carbon atom fewer
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Reagents and conditions:** bromine and aqueous sodium hydroxide (sodium bromate(I) formed in situ), warmed gently. The carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate, so the amine has **one carbon fewer** than the amide.

$$\mathrm{RCONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \to RNH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O}$$

For example ethanamide, $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}$, gives methylamine, $\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}$ (not ethylamine).

variantes.quand_utiliser: To convert an amide back to a carboxylic acid derivative, or to identify an amide
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Heating with dilute acid gives the carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt: $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2 + H_2O + HCl \to CH_3COOH + NH_4Cl}$.

Heating with aqueous sodium hydroxide gives the sodium salt of the acid and ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue: $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2 + NaOH \to CH_3COONa + NH_3}$. The free carboxylic acid is only obtained after acidifying the sodium salt.

variantes.quand_utiliser: To distinguish an aliphatic primary amine from an aromatic primary amine
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Nitrous acid is made in the flask from sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid.

- An aliphatic primary amine at room temperature gives nitrogen gas (effervescence) and an alcohol: $\mathrm{C_3H_7NH_2 + HNO_2 \to C_3H_7OH + N_2 + H_2O}$.
- An aromatic primary amine such as phenylamine, kept below 5 °C, gives a diazonium salt that stays in solution. Adding it to an alkaline solution of phenol or 2-naphthol produces a coloured azo dye (coupling reaction).

sections.enonce_markdown: Propanamide, $\mathrm{C_2H_5CONH_2}$, is warmed with bromine and aqueous sodium hydroxide. (a) Write the balanced equation and name the organic product. (b) A student starts with 14.6 g of propanamide and obtains 80% of the maximum possible mass of the amine. Calculate the mass of amine obtained. (c) Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide needed to react completely with 14.6 g of propanamide. (H = 1.0, C = 12.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0)

etapes.action: Write the balanced equation for the Hofmann degradation.
etapes.justification: The amide loses its carbonyl carbon as carbonate, so the amine has one carbon fewer than the amide.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $\mathrm{C_2H_5CONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \to C_2H_5NH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O}$. The product is $\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}$, **ethanamine** (ethylamine).

etapes.justification: The amount in moles is mass divided by molar mass.

etapes.action: Find the theoretical mass of ethanamine.
etapes.justification: The equation shows 1 mol of amide gives 1 mol of amine.
Only 80% of the theoretical mass is actually obtained.

etapes.action: Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide required.
etapes.justification: The equation shows 4 mol of NaOH per mole of amide, and the reagent is needed for the complete conversion (100% basis).

sections.conclusion_markdown: The product is ethanamine; the student obtains **7.20 g**, and **32.0 g** of sodium hydroxide are needed for complete reaction of 14.6 g of propanamide.

items.erreur_markdown: "The Hofmann degradation of propanamide gives propylamine."
items.pourquoi_faux: The carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate, so the amine has one carbon fewer than the amide. The amide carbon chain is shortened, never kept.
items.correction_markdown: Propanamide ($\mathrm{C_3}$) gives ethylamine ($\mathrm{C_2}$). Count the carbons: amine = amide minus one.

items.erreur_markdown: "Ethanamide is a base like the amines because it contains an NH2 group."
items.pourquoi_faux: In an amide the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl group and is no longer available to accept a proton. Amides are neutral.
items.correction_markdown: Amides do not turn litmus blue and do not form salts with dilute acids at room temperature; amines do.

items.erreur_markdown: "Phenylamine is a stronger base than ethylamine because the benzene ring is electron-rich."
items.pourquoi_faux: The nitrogen lone pair of phenylamine is delocalised into the ring, which makes it less available to accept a proton. In ethylamine the alkyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen.
items.correction_markdown: Order of base strength: ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine.

items.erreur_markdown: "Heating ethanamide with aqueous sodium hydroxide gives ethanoic acid and ammonia."
items.pourquoi_faux: In alkaline solution the acid formed is immediately neutralised, so the organic product is the sodium salt, not the free acid.
items.correction_markdown: $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2 + NaOH \to CH_3COONa + NH_3}$. Ethanoic acid is obtained only after the mixture is acidified.

items.erreur_markdown: "Bromoethane and ammonia give only ethylamine, whatever the proportions."
items.pourquoi_faux: Ethylamine is itself a nucleophile and attacks more bromoethane, giving a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt.
items.correction_markdown: Use a large excess of ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube, so that a bromoethane molecule is much more likely to meet ammonia than an amine.

items.enonce_markdown: Classify each compound as a primary, secondary or tertiary amine, an amide, or other, and name it: (i) $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NHCH_3}$; (ii) $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}$; (iii) $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CONH_2}$; (iv) $\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(i) Nitrogen carries two carbon groups: **secondary amine**, N-methylethanamine.

(ii) Nitrogen carries three carbon groups: **tertiary amine**, trimethylamine (N,N-dimethylmethanamine).

(iii) The $\mathrm{-CONH_2}$ group is present: **primary amide**, propanamide.

(iv) Nitrogen carries one carbon group, an aryl group: **primary aromatic amine**, phenylamine.

items.enonce_markdown: (H = 1.0, C = 12.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0, Na = 23.0; molar volume 24 $\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$ at r.t.p.) A sample of 2.95 g of ethanamide is heated with an excess of aqueous sodium hydroxide until the reaction is complete. (a) Write the balanced equation. (b) Calculate the volume of ammonia gas released at r.t.p. (c) Calculate the mass of sodium ethanoate formed.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2 + NaOH \to CH_3COONa + NH_3}$ (each side has 2 C, 6 H, 1 N, 2 O and 1 Na).

(b) $M_r(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}) = 2\times12.0 + 5\times1.0 + 14.0 + 16.0 = 59.0$, so $n = 2.95/59.0 = 0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}$. The equation gives 1 mol of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ per mole of amide, so $V = 0.0500\times24 = $ **$1.20\ \mathrm{dm^3}$**.

(c) $M_r(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}) = 2\times12.0 + 3\times1.0 + 2\times16.0 + 23.0 = 82.0$; mass $= 0.0500\times82.0 = $ **$4.10\ \mathrm{g}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: (H = 1.0, C = 12.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0, Cl = 35.5; molar volume 24 $\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$ at r.t.p.) Compound X, of molecular formula $\mathrm{C_4H_9NO}$, has an unbranched carbon chain. Warming X with bromine and aqueous sodium hydroxide gives Y, of formula $\mathrm{C_3H_9N}$, which gives off nitrogen gas when treated with nitrous acid at room temperature. (a) Identify X and Y and give the type of reaction that converts X to Y. (b) Y from 8.70 g of X (complete conversion) is dissolved in excess dilute hydrochloric acid. Calculate the mass of the salt formed. (c) Calculate the volume of nitrogen at r.t.p. obtained if the same amount of Y were treated with excess nitrous acid.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) X is an amide because Hofmann degradation turns an amide into an amine with one carbon fewer: $\mathrm{C_4H_9NO}$ (4 carbons, unbranched) gives a three-carbon amine $\mathrm{C_3H_9N}$. Nitrogen with nitrous acid shows a primary aliphatic amine. **X is butanamide, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CONH_2}$; Y is propan-1-amine, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}$; the reaction is the Hofmann degradation.**

(b) $M_r(\mathrm{X}) = 4\times12.0 + 9\times1.0 + 14.0 + 16.0 = 87.0$; $n = 8.70/87.0 = 0.100\ \mathrm{mol}$. Y reacts with HCl 1:1 to give propylammonium chloride $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_3Cl}$, $M_r = 3\times12.0 + 10\times1.0 + 14.0 + 35.5 = 95.5$. Mass $= 0.100\times95.5 = $ **$9.55\ \mathrm{g}$**.

(c) $\mathrm{C_3H_7NH_2 + HNO_2 \to C_3H_7OH + N_2 + H_2O}$ gives 1 mol of $\mathrm{N_2}$ per mole of amine, so $V = 0.100\times24 = $ **$2.40\ \mathrm{dm^3}$**.

items_markdown: Amines are classified by the number of carbon groups on nitrogen; an amide contains the -CONH2 group.
Amines are weak bases (lone pair on N): ethylamine > ammonia > phenylamine; amides are neutral because the lone pair is delocalised onto C=O.
A halogenoalkane gives a primary amine only with a large excess of ethanolic ammonia (sealed tube); nitriles are reduced to primary amines with LiAlH4 in dry ether.
Hofmann degradation: RCONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH gives RNH2 + Na2CO3 + 2NaBr + 2H2O, so the amine has one carbon fewer than the amide.
Amides hydrolyse to the carboxylic acid (hot dilute acid, ammonium salt) or to the carboxylate salt and NH3 (hot NaOH).
Nitrous acid: aliphatic primary amines give N2 gas at room temperature; aromatic primary amines below 5 °C give diazonium salts that couple to form azo dyes.
